name: CFPB: Final Rule on Quality Control Standards for Automated Valuation Models
title: CFPB: Final Rule on Quality Control Standards for Automated Valuation Models
answer: The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau publishes this final rule page on quality control standards for automated valuation models. It says the CFPB, OCC, FRB, FDIC, NCUA and FHFA adopted a Dodd-Frank mandated rule for AVMs used by mortgage originators and secondary market issuers to determine the collateral worth of a mortgage secured by a consumer's principal dwelling. The most useful point is that covered institutions must adopt policies, practices, procedures and control systems, including random sample testing and reviews, so AVM estimates meet quality control standards.

sections.body: The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau publishes this page as a final rule notice. It covers quality control standards for automated valuation models used by mortgage originators and secondary market issuers in determining the collateral worth of a mortgage secured by a consumer's principal dwelling. The page states that the CFPB, OCC, FRB, FDIC, NCUA and FHFA adopted the final rule to implement standards mandated by the Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act. The supplied text does not state a publication or effective date. It is a regulatory summary page rather than a research report or industry guide.
sections.heading: What this source is

sections.body: The page says the final rule implements quality control standards for the use of automated valuation models by mortgage originators and secondary market issuers in determining the collateral worth of a mortgage secured by a consumer's principal dwelling. It states that six agencies, the CFPB, OCC, FRB, FDIC, NCUA and FHFA, adopted the final rule to implement quality control standards mandated by the Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act. Under the rule, institutions that engage in certain credit decisions or securitization determinations must adopt policies, practices, procedures and control systems. These are meant to ensure that AVMs used in these transactions to determine the value of mortgage collateral adhere to quality control standards. The page lists standards designed to ensure a high level of confidence in the estimates produced by AVMs, protect against the manipulation of data, seek to avoid conflicts of interest, require random sample testing and reviews, and comply with app. The supplied text ends mid-sentence at 'comply with app', so the final item is incomplete. The page repeats its opening summary sentence twice.
sections.heading: What it says

sections.body: The text gives no numeric figures. It names six agencies: the CFPB, OCC, FRB, FDIC, NCUA and FHFA. It defines the rule's scope as the use of automated valuation models by mortgage originators and secondary market issuers in determining the collateral worth of a mortgage secured by a consumer's principal dwelling. It says the standards are mandated by the Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act. It lists quality control goals: a high level of confidence in AVM estimates, protection against data manipulation, avoiding conflicts of interest, random sample testing and reviews, and compliance with app, with the last item cut off in the supplied text.
sections.heading: Figures and claims worth noting

sections.body: For a reader following AI in real estate, this source is the federal regulatory record for automated valuation models in mortgage lending. It shows that AVM use by mortgage originators and secondary market issuers is subject to joint agency quality control standards, including policies, procedures, control systems, random sample testing and reviews. It is useful for understanding how valuation models and model accountability are supervised, even though the supplied text does not use the term artificial intelligence. It also identifies the agencies involved, which helps a reader trace which bodies supervise this area.
sections.heading: What it means for AI in Real Estate

sections.body: The supplied text is a short regulatory summary page, not the full rule. It does not state a publication date, effective date, compliance date, enforcement provisions or definitions beyond the scope sentence. It does not mention artificial intelligence, machine learning, real estate brokerage or non mortgage uses of AVMs. It ends mid-sentence at 'comply with app', so one listed standard is incomplete. The page is government published rather than commercial, but it is partial and repeats its opening sentence. A reader needing the complete standards would need the full rule text.
